title_original: Debora Brune Makes Beauty of the Scars We Carry

blocks.text: With Uncool , her first book, fashion photographer Debora Brune, herself a wheelchair user, spent four years meeting and portraying models whose injured, ailing, or disabled bodies fall outside the norm.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Debora Brune.

Their disabilities are physical or sensory, present from birth or arriving with an accident or an illness. Fikayo’s blind eye is clouded a milky white. Beneath her hearing aid, Sophie has slipped a Vivienne Westwood earring, matched like a jewel. Caitlin has painted the toenails of her prosthetic leg with the same care as the rest. Lauren sits, sovereign, in her wheelchair. Scars, vitiligo, albinism, amputations: here, difference is shown without voyeurism and without pity.

Debora Brune came up through fashion before turning toward a more conceptual practice, probing the way bodies are seen, sorted, and made to behave. In 2026, she won the Dior Photography and Visual Arts Award at the Rencontres d’Arles. Her work, as Gui—who is albino and visually impaired—puts it, “captures individuals in their uniqueness, their beauty, and their abilities.” She does not soften what sets her subjects apart; she builds the beauty of the image around it. Natalie-Amber, a survivor of fulminant sepsis who now devotes her work to women everywhere, understood the gesture at once: “our body is our home, and we are beautiful just as we are.”

An ode to the sheer variety of bodies and their startling beauty, Uncool reveals the flesh with as much tenderness as nerve. Grace has worn a port-wine birthmark on the right side of her face since the day she was born. Catrin , burned across most of her body when a coach crashed in the Alps at nineteen, stands tall in a Burberry bikini. Debora Brune counts herself among her models, photographing her own back cleaved by a long white scar. These are bodies of pure presence. “My scars are a part of me, but they are not all of me,” Emma says. “To live with scarring on display can be terrifying, strong, upsetting, uplifting—but ultimately, it is part of you.”

Kjell is an actor. His drooping eyelid earned him a lifetime of people swearing he’d never make it in the business. He has learned not to give a damn. In the book he holds the camera’s eye, his gaze faintly veiled, his lips parted: “I no longer want to explain myself as a body.” J unior grew up in southeast London without ever once seeing a wheelchair user on television, in a schoolbook, or on the street. He went on to address the Houses of Parliament on the lack of workplace access and the way society looks at disability. “My existence shouldn’t make you uncomfortable. If I can find beauty and pride in myself and this world—so can you.”
Uncool by Debora Brune is self-published and available for €55.
Debora Brune will present the book and sign copies on Thursday, October 15, 2026, from 6 to 10 p.m. at the Open Space gallery in Berlin, Germany.
